model_annotation: Figure 2 displays a horizontal bar chart titled “Negative log-probabilities for clinically relevant tokens between baseline Mistral-v0.2 and the same model further fine-tuned on each specialty data,” illustrating the average negative log-probabilities of medical terms across six clinical specialties: Cardio, Gastro, Infect, Neuro, Obstetrics, and Pediatrics. Each specialty is represented by a distinct color-coded bar, with the bar length corresponding to the magnitude of the negative log-probability — longer bars indicate higher (worse) negative log-probabilities, meaning lower predicted token probabilities. The chart visually compares two model variants per specialty: the baseline Mistral-v0.2 (lighter shade) and its fine-tuned variant on that specialty’s data (darker shade). Across all six specialties, the darker bars are consistently shorter than their lighter counterparts, indicating that fine-tuning on specialty-specific data reduces the negative log-probability — i.e., improves the model’s confidence in predicting clinically relevant terms. The x-axis is labeled “Per-specialty terms” and represents the negative log-probability scale, though no explicit numerical tick labels are shown; the relative lengths of the bars convey the comparative improvement. The chart’s layout and color coding emphasize that fine-tuning leads to domain-specific adaptation rather than the injection of new domain knowledge, supporting the paper’s hypothesis that performance gains stem from domain shifting.
